kernel_family_characterization.regime_bo.reason: Three explicit rankings identify the regimes. At matched success probability, parity-capped f2 is cheapest in 18/18 reachable cells, and below about 1e-3 at n_k<=6 no member of that class is feasible. By N_gates/sqrt(P), parity-capped f2 wins at every eps>=1e-2.5 and the rational f_jy wins at every eps<=1e-3 (by 1.35x at (8,1e-4)), so the crossover is at about 1e-3. By raw gates, uncapped f2 or f_jy wins. Exact kernels never win. Feasibility boundaries follow from the FCC resolution law k_max <~ 2(N_k-1)/ln(C/eps): reference floors are 3.6e-3 at n_k=6 and 3.0e-4 at n_k=7. Each boundary is tied to analytical structure: Gaussian vs stretched-exponential tails, the pole at -i, and the one-norm cap.

mechanism_analysis.subsection_present.reason: Sec 6.1 is an explicit mechanism subsection: 'Mechanism: why f2 is the right kernel for this circuit at these resolutions'.

mechanism_analysis.depth.reason: The analysis ties the kernel's structure to the observed gate scaling inside the framework. The selector carries at least 93.3% of gates, so the gate ratio is roughly the truncation-radius ratio, corrected by 1+c/(td). Gaussian vs stretched-exponential tails set k_max, at the price of the scalar error at the conserved mode. The FCC pole-at--i resolution law favours small radii and sets the k-register needed. Phase absorption into the B_m block-encoding gives real positive weights, so one even QSVT suffices, with degree ~ k_max ln(1/delta) set by the branch points at +/-i/k_max. Together this explains why FCC plus single-QSP fits this kernel.

mechanism_analysis.optimality_explained.reason: 'Why not the other families' uses the characterisation data to explain the choice. ACL beta=0.9 has alpha=2.01 without a smaller radius. Cauchy is feasible only at eps >~ 1e-2. Uncapped f2 and f_jy have smaller radii but P of 0.08-0.27 and 0.17-0.33, and f_jy needs complex weights. Parity-capped f2 is best for the one-shot circuit as specified because it is Gaussian-tailed, real-weighted and tunable to the reference one-norm. The paper also states honestly where f_jy wins: below 1e-3 if the whole circuit is amplitude-amplified.

failure_analysis.patterns_identified.reason: The patterns are concrete. There is no exponent gain over [1e-4, 1e-1.5], with c shrinking from 0.7 to 0.35. At t=0.05 the selector is 13% longer. QSVT weights cost up to 2.0x more outside the selector at 1e-4, and brute force is cheaper at the n_k=7 headline. Rejected choices are listed: c=0, compact mollifiers, a fixed-c rule and the LS cost-optimal point.

failure_analysis.patterns_explained_cohe.reason: Each pattern is tied to a specific kernel or implementation feature: erfc(1/2gamma)->1 and the one-norm cap forcing c down while k_max ~ 2 ln(1/eps)/c; bound looseness from |1+z^2| ~ y0^2 on the shifted contour; the FCC resolution law at small n_k; the c/t diagonal shift relative to ||A_L||t; brute-force cost ~ 2^n_k vs QSVT ~ d n_k with d ~ k_max ln(1/delta); and the ACL no-go result for compactly supported mollifiers. The robustness checks were tested and documented (A7, A8).

It also adds a one-QSVT exact-AA weight preparation, an FCC 'resolution law' (described as the angle-variable counterpart of LS's estimate), and the first end-to-end emulated comparison and family map in this framework. This is a meaningful extension rather than replication or a distinct new kernel.
